name: Grimm's Law
statement: The Germanic languages shifted their consonants in a regular chain away from their Indo-European roots.
meaning: A set of regular sound changes by which the stop consonants of Proto-Indo-European systematically shifted in the Germanic branch. Voiceless stops like p, t, and k became fricatives f, th, and h; voiced stops b, d, and g became voiceless p, t, and k; and the breathy voiced stops became plain voiced b, d, and g. This is why English words inherited from Germanic differ predictably from their Latin and Greek cousins.
mechanism: The three parts interlock as a chain shift, the First Germanic Consonant Shift. As the voiced stops moved into the slots vacated by the voiceless stops, those voiceless stops had already moved on to fricatives, and the breathy stops filled the emptied voiced slots. The changes are word-independent and systematic, applying across the whole vocabulary rather than to particular words — which is exactly what marks the Germanic languages off from the rest of Indo-European.

examples.text: Latin pater and pes correspond to English father and foot, because Proto-Indo-European p shifted to f in Germanic — while borrowed Latin words like paternal keep the original p.
Latin tres corresponds to English three, the t having shifted to the th sound in the Germanic branch.
Latin cornu corresponds to English horn, and Latin duo to English two, showing the k-to-h and d-to-t steps of the shift.

variants.name: Verner's law
variants.text: The 1875 discovery that explains the systematic exceptions to Grimm's law: certain shifted consonants became voiced when the preceding syllable did not carry the old Indo-European accent, a hidden regularity behind apparent irregularity.

variants.name: The Second Germanic Consonant Shift
variants.text: A later, separate shift affecting only High German, giving pairs like English water beside German Wasser and English apple beside German Apfel.

whyItMatters: It was a foundational discovery of historical linguistics, demonstrating that sound change is regular and systematic rather than haphazard, and grounding the comparative method for reconstructing ancestral languages. Together with Verner's law, it became the showcase for the principle that sound laws admit no exceptions.

working.text: expect an inherited Germanic word to differ from its Latin or Greek cognate by these regular consonant correspondences.
recognise Latin-derived loanwords in English by their unshifted consonants, which entered too late to undergo the shift.
when a correspondence seems irregular, check whether Verner's law and the old accent placement explain it.

limits: Grimm's law has systematic apparent exceptions, where a Proto-Indo-European voiceless stop became a voiced fricative rather than the predicted voiceless one. These were resolved by Verner's law in 1875: the outcome depended on where the old Indo-European word-accent fell, an accent later obscured when Germanic fixed stress on the first syllable. Far from undermining the law, this deepened it, turning apparent irregularity into a further regular law — a landmark vindication of the principle that sound change is exceptionless.
misreadings: It does not apply to words English borrowed from Latin or Greek — those keep their original consonants, having entered after the shift; it governs only the inherited Germanic vocabulary. And its exceptions are not true irregularities but the workings of Verner's law, conditioned by an accent since lost.
origin: Formulated as a general rule by Jacob Grimm in the second edition of his Deutsche Grammatik (1822); the correspondences had been noted earlier by Rasmus Rask around 1818 and, in part, by Friedrich von Schlegel in 1806, making it a case where the systematiser, not the first observer, gave it his name.
